steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A perspective or viewpoint is the writer's attitude, opinion or stance on a subject. It's what they think or feel about the topic they're writing about.

steps.title: Word Connotations
steps.body: The feelings and associations words evoke "Stubborn" vs "determined" - same behaviour, different attitude

steps.title: Emotive Language
steps.body: Words designed to provoke emotional responses "Murder" vs "killing" vs "death" - different emotional weights

steps.title: Bias
steps.body: A tendency to favour one side or perspective, often unfairly.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What is the difference between perspective and bias? | Name three language features that might reveal a writer's perspective. | How can word connotations show perspective?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Perspective is a writer's viewpoint or opinion; bias is when that perspective unfairly favours one side, often by misrepresenting or ignoring opposing views. | Emotive language, word connotations, tone, direct statements, rhetorical devices. | Words with positive connotations show approval; negative connotations show disapproval. The choice reveals the writer's attitude toward the subject.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Look for emotive language and word choice Identify the writer's attitude, not just their opinion Support with specific quotations Consider WHY the writer holds this view Think about context - when and why was this written? Look for bias and subjectivity Consider what's included AND what's left out
